message.content: When Copernicus developed heliocentrism, Europe was still dominated by scholastic theology and the Church's Ptolemaic cosmology. Poland was relatively stable under the Jagiellonian dynasty, while the Holy Roman Empire and papal politics remained tense amid the Renaissance and Reformation. Printers spread classical texts, but astronomical ideas still required patronage, church approval, and cautious wording. His cactiform model of celestial order, though mathematically elegant, challenged geocentric assumptions and imperial religious expectations. Thus his theory emerged not from a free scientific revolution but from a fragile mix of scholarship, diplomacy, and confessional conflict.
